chunks.title: Who Vineeth is
chunks.text: Vineeth Reddy Kodakandla is an ML engineer based in the United States who works on model inference and evaluation: how fast and how cheaply models run on real hardware, and whether their output holds up. He completed an M.S. in Computer Science at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi (August 2024 to May 2026). Before that he worked on LLM serving at EXL (Noida, India, 2023 to 2024) and on real-time vision inference at L&T Technology Services (Bengaluru, India, 2022 to 2023). His public projects are measurement studies: bitwise-forensics, which measures whether a continuous-batching engine returns the same greedy tokens when requests are batched together; the Meteor Lake Latency Lab, which measures which processor on an Intel laptop chip should run live instance segmentation; and the LLM Eval Observatory, a nightly evaluation of open-weight models on anti-money-laundering alert triage. Every measured result on his site links to the committed file it came from.

chunks.title: Roles he is looking for
chunks.text: Vineeth is looking for ML engineer, inference engineer and software engineering roles, especially work on model serving, performance and evaluation. He is based in the United States and open to relocating anywhere in the US. The best way to start a conversation is email at vineethkodakandla@gmail.com.

chunks.title: FAQ: work authorization and sponsorship
chunks.text: Vineeth is authorized to work in the United States now, on F-1 OPT following his M.S. in Computer Science at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. To continue beyond OPT he will need H-1B sponsorship, and he would rather talk about timing early in a process than late. Roles that require US citizenship or a security clearance are not a fit.

chunks.title: Project: bitwise-forensics (token changes under continuous batching)
chunks.text:
bitwise-forensics is Vineeth's LLM-serving measurement project (public repository github.com/vineethkodakandla/bitwise-forensics, version 0.3.1; case study on this site at /work/bitwise-forensics). It asks whether a serving engine returns the same greedy tokens for a prompt when other requests share its engine steps. He measured OpenVINO GenAI 2026.3's ContinuousBatchingPipeline serving Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct with INT4 weights, greedy decoding and up to 128 new tokens, on the Arc iGPU and the CPU of an Intel Core Ultra 7 155H. The prompts are 40 short instructions built from 4 templates and 10 LLM-serving topics. Each prompt is served alone for a batch-of-1 reference, then all 40 arrive on Poisson schedules and share engine steps. Load is an arrival rate from c2 to c32, meaning arrivals per maximum-length generation on a virtual clock of 20 ms engine steps; it is not a number of users. Every device and option set sees the same arrival schedules, although batches at later steps can differ once outputs stop at different lengths, and prefill options change how requests are grouped into steps even when output lengths match. Each configuration ran 8 trials, so each row covers 320 runs: 12 configurations make 3,840 runs per device and 7,680 in total.

Under default settings, a batched run's tokens differed from the same prompt's batch-of-1 output in 95.6 to 100 percent of iGPU runs and 54.4 to 72.5 percent of CPU runs. The two devices run different quantized defaults (iGPU: f16 activations, 4-bit KV cache, dynamic quantization group size 32; CPU: f32 activations, 8-bit KV cache, dynamic quantization group size 32), so the difference between them is not a hardware comparison. On the CPU the share rose from c2 to c4 by 18.1 points (95% CI 5.3 to 30.3); the two comparisons made beyond c4 (c16 against c4 and c32 against c8) detected no change.

Replaying the eight c8 arrival schedules with default options, in the same process, reproduced all 320 runs on each device bit for bit (tokens, chosen-token logprobs and per-step batch sizes), and batch-of-1 output was bitwise identical across repeated passes for every option set. So where tested, the output was a fixed function of the arrival schedule, and a different schedule could change it.

On the CPU at c8, turning off dynamic activation quantization cut the share of runs with changed tokens from 71.2 to 21.2 percent (paired 95% CI for the drop: 34.7 to 64.4 points). An f32 KV cache alone had no detectable effect on the share (+0.3 points, paired 95% CI -14.7 to +15.0). With both settings, 0 of 320 runs had changed tokens at c8 and 0 of 320 at c32; the exact 95% upper bound is 8.8 percent counting prompts and 1.1 percent counting runs. That setting is not batch-invariant, because chosen-token logprobs still differed from batch-of-1 in every one of those runs, by at most 2.9e-5. Capping each engine step at 16 tokens (max_num_batched_tokens=16, a budget shared with decode tokens, so prompts are split across several steps) raised the CPU c8 share from 71.2 to 90.0 percent (paired difference +18.8 points, 95% CI 5.3 to 32.2); that option also changed batch-of-1 output on 36 of 40 CPU prompts. On the iGPU no tested setting removed the token changes: an f16 KV cache lowered the c8 share to 51.2 percent, turning off dynamic quantization left it at 100 percent, and none of the eight builds given the f32 inference precision hint served even one 2-token request in this OpenVINO GenAI version with this driver (two did not compile, four failed on the first engine step and two on the second).

Method: per-row bootstrap intervals over prompts and trials widened to exact Clopper-Pearson intervals; paired comparisons on identical arrival schedules; a replay control; batch-of-1 checks before and after the trials; committed per-token results, scripts that recompute the scorecards and README statistics from them, and a README that traces every result to a committed file or to a separate precision probe; and 186 tests in CI on Linux and Windows. The project began as a simulator; across 12 simulator seeds (each changing the synthetic model, its noise streams and the arrival schedules) its load trend changed direction, so the simulator is kept only as a pipeline test. Stated limits: one engine, one small model, one laptop, greedy decoding, 40 short templated prompts, no measurement of output quality (so nothing about batched outputs being better or worse), no attribution to a specific operation, no comparison with other engines, and intervals not adjusted for multiple comparisons.

chunks.title: Project: Meteor Lake Latency Lab (edge inference latency)
chunks.text:
The Meteor Lake Latency Lab is Vineeth's edge-inference project (public repository github.com/vineethkodakandla/edge-vision-lab; case study on this site at /work/meteor-lake-latency-lab). It asks which processor on one laptop chip, an Intel Core Ultra 7 155H, should run live instance segmentation within a 33.3 ms per-frame budget: the NPU, the Arc integrated GPU or the CPU. The model is YOLOv8n-seg at a fixed 640 by 640 input through OpenVINO 2026.3, in FP32, FP16 and two INT8 builds made with NNCF post-training quantization on 300 COCO val2017 images. One INT8 build keeps the detection-head decode in float and the other quantizes everything. Accuracy is measured on the other 4,700 images. The benchmark discards 100 warm-up frames and times 1,000 frames per configuration with 45 s cooldowns, covering preprocess, inference and the host-side postprocess (NumPy decode with OpenCV NMS).

In the flat-out benchmark, INT8 on the iGPU had an 11.3 ms median but a 47.0 ms p99, while INT8 on the NPU had a 13.9 ms median and an 18.0 ms p99. On a live webcam loop (one 60 s session each, 2,398 iGPU frames and 1,891 NPU frames; the loop does not wait for new camera frames) the iGPU ran a 10.4 ms median and 13.3 ms p99, ahead of the NPU at 18.0 ms and 22.3 ms, although it missed the budget on 8 of 2,398 frames (0.33 percent) against the NPU's 1 of 1,891 (0.05 percent). So the p99 order of the two accelerators reverses with how busy they are kept, while the median favoured the iGPU and the budget-miss rate favoured the NPU in both measured runs. The CPU was not run live. The iGPU's flat-out tail came from CPU-side stalls, defined as frames where preprocess plus postprocess took more than 20 ms: the iGPU produced 63 stall frames in 4,000 against 6 for the NPU and 1 for the CPU, and without stall frames the iGPU INT8 p99 is 17.1 ms while its inference-only p99 was 9.5 ms. The cause of the stalls is not attributed; separating display compositor contention, the shared package power budget and driver threads would need ETW tracing.

Keeping the detection-head decode in float cost 0.0015 box mAP on the CPU; quantizing everything cost 0.0389, about 26 times as much. What the fully quantized build bought in speed depended on the processor: its NPU median was only 0.35 ms faster, its iGPU median was 1.33 ms faster but with a worse flat-out p99 (49.0 against 47.0 ms), and on the CPU it cut the frames over budget from 46.3 to 4.8 percent. INT8 cost 0.0024 box mAP on the iGPU and 0.0023 on the NPU against the CPU FP32 reference. Stated limits: power was not measured; one model and input size on one machine; only the two INT8 configurations were run live, for one session each; and because the live loop does not wait for new camera frames, it ran busier than a strict 30 fps camera.

chunks.title: Project: LLM Eval Observatory (nightly LLM evaluation)
chunks.text:
The LLM Eval Observatory is Vineeth's evaluation project (public repository github.com/vineethkodakandla/llm-eval-observatory, dashboard llm-eval-observatory.vercel.app; case study on this site at /work/llm-eval-observatory). A GitHub Action runs nightly against open-weight models on Groq's free tier and commits latest.json and history.jsonl back to the repository, and a Next.js dashboard on Vercel reads them. The main track asks whether a model can triage anti-money-laundering alerts: 26 hand-written synthetic cases (14 escalate, 8 clear, 4 review), each answered as ESCALATE, CLEAR or REVIEW with cited evidence, and scored by a deterministic parser rather than by another model. It reports decision accuracy, typology accuracy, citation faithfulness, fabricated-citation rate, false-clear rate (clearing a case that should have been escalated, the dangerous miss) and whether ambiguous cases are sent to review. The other tracks are a 30-prompt injection and jailbreak battery in which quoting the payload counts as a breach, a 50-item capability set with drift detection, and an LLM-as-judge reliability check on 24 human-labelled pairwise items using Cohen's and Fleiss' kappa. Decision accuracy, injection defense, capability accuracy and judge agreement carry percentile bootstrap intervals with 5,000 seeded resamples; the false-clear rate and the other rates are exact ratios without an interval. A drift flag, computed for decision accuracy, injection defense and capability accuracy, fires only when the score moves at least 5 points and the intervals do not overlap, compared with the most recent run that produced results; a night where every model is skipped does not overwrite earlier results.

From 2 August to 15 September 2026, GPT-OSS 120B completed the triage track on 29 nights and never cleared a case that should have been escalated, with accuracy between 92.3 and 100 percent on the same cases. Counting from the first live run on 28 July, it defended 93.3 to 96.7 percent of injection attacks over 31 nights, and Llama 3.3 70B defended 73.3 to 83.3 percent over the 19 nights it completed, the last on 17 August. Groq's deprecations page lists both Llama models as shut down on 16 August 2026, and every nightly run from 18 August got HTTP 404 for them. On 15 September 2026 the configuration was cut from 5 models to GPT-OSS 20B and GPT-OSS 120B, the only production open-weight chat models left on Groq's free tier. The case study page shows the latest run live. When Groq no longer serves a model, rejects its requests or keeps rate-limiting it, that model is dropped for the rest of the run. Stated limits: the cases are synthetic and self-authored, so this is not a compliance benchmark; samples are small (4 ambiguous cases, so review routing moves in 25-point steps); several scores sit at the ceiling, and on recent nights both GPT-OSS judges agreed with every human label; the judges come from one vendor; and drift is compared only with the most recent run that produced results.

chunks.title: Project: Edith (multi-agent pipeline with a release gate)
chunks.text: Edith is a browser demo of a multi-agent pipeline (live at vineethkodakandla.github.io/edith-lab, source github.com/vineethkodakandla/edith-lab). Researcher, Analyst, Critic and Synthesizer agents run in a fixed order over a shared blackboard. The Critic runs before any draft is written: with a Groq key it reviews the Analyst's output, and by default it returns REVISE only when retrieval found nothing. A REVISE verdict makes the Synthesizer rewrite its draft once. A rule-based Governor then checks the final draft. If a check fails, the Synthesizer rewrites once more and the Governor checks again. A goal where retrieval found no document sharing a keyword always ends labelled blocked, needing human review, and the answer is still shown under that label. Apart from requiring retrieved sources, the Governor only tests the text for an action word such as recommend, proceed or defer (a plain substring match). It never checks that the text agrees with the sources, so an off-topic keyword match can pass. By default it is deterministic, retrieving by term-frequency cosine similarity over an 8-document built-in corpus. The code also has an optional mode in which the agents call Llama 3.1 8B and Llama 3.3 70B on Groq with a visitor's own key, but Groq shut those models down on 16 August 2026, so that mode fails until its model IDs are updated. The Governor is rule-based in both modes. It is written as framework-free JavaScript modules with no build step. It is a small demo of orchestration and a release gate, not a production system.

chunks.title: Project: ANANTA (agent memory that forgets)
chunks.text: ANANTA is a browser demo of agent memory that forgets on purpose (live at vineethkodakandla.github.io/ananta-lab, source github.com/vineethkodakandla/ananta-lab). Each memory decays on an Ebbinghaus forgetting curve, each recall raises the memory's stability, and a manual decay pass prunes memories whose retention has fallen below 2 percent, unless their importance is 0.8 or higher. Every write chains a SHA-256 hash, through Web Crypto, of the memory's text, timestamp and importance, so editing any of those makes verification fail; tags and recall counts are not covered. A deterministic agent loop sits on top: lexical retrieval over 8 built-in documents, keyword-scored difficulty bands that pick a model tier, and a self-check that flags thin retrieval and escalates a tier. It still answers from the closest document and abstains only when no document matches at all. Its optional mode calls Llama 3.1 8B and Llama 3.3 70B on Groq for the draft step with a visitor's own key, but Groq shut those models down on 16 August 2026, so that mode fails until its model IDs are updated. It is a small, inspectable demo rather than a production memory system.

chunks.title: This site and its assistant
chunks.text: This portfolio site is a Next.js application deployed on Vercel (source github.com/vineethkodakandla/vineeth-portfolio). Its assistant answers from a short knowledge base written to match the pages, using retrieval-augmented generation: each question is embedded with Voyage, the closest passages are found by cosine search with pgvector in a Neon Postgres database, and Claude writes the answer from those passages, which are listed under the answer when retrieval succeeds; otherwise the whole knowledge base is used. The case-study chart values are copied from the projects' committed result files, and each chart links to the file its values came from, pinned to a commit. The LLM Eval Observatory panel reads that project's latest results file and refreshes at most hourly.

chunks.title: Experience: EXL (2023 to 2024)
chunks.text: From 2023 to 2024 Vineeth worked at EXL in Noida, India, on LLM serving for insurance underwriting and claims work. He worked on the Amazon Bedrock serving path (prompt routing, context-window management and token streaming), on evaluation runs that compared fine-tuned models with commercial models, and on the latency and cost dashboards the team used. He contributed pre-launch engineering to LDS Underwriting Assist, which EXL launched in August 2024. Outcomes EXL has published for that product are company results, not his personal metrics. Figures from his own work there are internal and are not published on this site; for more detail, contact him directly.

chunks.title: Experience: L&T Technology Services (2022 to 2023)
chunks.text: From 2022 to 2023 Vineeth worked at L&T Technology Services in Bengaluru, India, on real-time inference for endoscopy video, covering image enhancement and polyp detection, using NVIDIA's Holoscan SDK and developer kits. He moved models from PyTorch to ONNX Runtime and TensorRT, enabling FP16 where supported, restructured the input pipeline to reduce per-frame latency, and wrote the benchmarking scripts used to compare edge targets. He started there as an intern. Figures from that work are internal and are not published on this site; for more detail, contact him directly.

chunks.title: Education and certification
chunks.text: Vineeth earned an M.S. in Computer Science at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi (August 2024 to May 2026). He was a graduate research assistant working on rule-based multi-agent access control with ABAC and XACML, and a teaching assistant for Computer Forensics. His coursework included computer architecture, advanced software engineering, network security and agent-based systems. He holds Anthropic's Building with the Claude API certification.

chunks.title: Tools and methods
chunks.text: Inference and optimization: OpenVINO and OpenVINO GenAI, NNCF post-training quantization, ONNX Runtime and TensorRT, FP16 and INT8 quantization, continuous batching. Measurement: latency distributions and frame budgets, bootstrap confidence intervals, paired comparisons, replay and reproducibility checks, benchmark automation. LLM applications and evaluation: evaluation harnesses, prompt-injection testing, LLM-as-judge reliability, retrieval-augmented generation, Amazon Bedrock. Engineering: Python, TypeScript, C++, SQL, NumPy, pandas, PyTorch, FastAPI, React, Next.js, PostgreSQL with pgvector, Docker, Kubernetes and GitHub Actions. The public projects show the inference, measurement and evaluation work end to end.

chunks.title: How he approaches problems
chunks.text: Vineeth's projects usually start from a claim that is easy to repeat and then check where it holds: that a benchmark picks the right processor for a camera, that greedy decoding gives the same tokens when requests are batched together, that a model can triage alerts without a person reading each one. The answer is usually that it depends, and the useful part is finding out on what. He publishes what a result does not show alongside what it does, and drops results that fail a check: bitwise-forensics began as a simulator and moved to a real engine after a check across 12 seeds showed that the simulated load trend was not stable.
